content.title: About
content.content: Carrots are a root vegetable from the Apiaceae family, cultivated in temperate climates. Mature raw carrots have a bright orange color, a mildly sweet taste, and a crunchy texture. They are eaten fresh, added to salads, juiced, and used as an ingredient in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were domesticated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.
The orange color was popularized by Dutch breeders in the 17th century.
There are more than 100 carrot varieties, including purple, yellow, and red types.
Beta‑carotene gives carrots their orange hue and is converted to vitamin A in the body.
Carrots can grow in low‑nitrogen soils but require good drainage.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is a precursor of vitamin A, essential for vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Fiber and potassium help lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improves digestion
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber promote gut motility and a healthy microbiome.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals enhance the body's defense mechanisms.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Excessive beta‑carotene intake
items.content: Very high consumption can cause carotenemia – a temporary yellowing of the skin.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Unwashed carrots may carry pesticide residues; it is advisable to wash them thoroughly before eating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Carrots can be eaten raw, sliced into sticks, grated, or added to salads. They are also used in juices, smoothies, and as garnish for various dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated bag. When kept properly, they stay fresh for 2–3 weeks. Remove the leafy tops, as they accelerate root spoilage.
